extracted.intended_audience: engineers, municipal planners, and scientifically literate general public (late-19th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for fairly comparing electric and coal-gas illumination systems on a commercial/industrial scale, including how to size plants, which cost items to include, and how to account for demand variability and distribution-system differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for a valuable comparison of illuminants
rubrics_metrics.description: A comparison, to be of any value, should be between plants of a size sufficient to reduce the cost to the lowest point at which it can be commercially maintained, and should include all of the items entering into it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not compare only material consumption or small-scale apparatus; adopt an industrial-scale basis and include all capital and operating cost items (plant, mains, distribution, apparatus, etc.) so the comparison reflects realistic commercial conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a sufficiently large (industrial) plant as the comparison unit
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparison is upon the basis of works capable of producing a million feet a day, as, in such works, gas can be made as cheaply as in any that are larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a representative large-scale production capacity (the author uses 1,000,000 cubic feet/day) so economies of scale are captured; avoid small-scale or limited-production bases that unfairly raise electricity costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all items entering into cost (capital and distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful comparison should include all of the items entering into [cost].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count plant construction, mains and feeders, distributing stations, engines/dynamos, boilers, installation of mains, and associated real-estate, installation and (implicitly) depreciation/maintenance and fuel costs when comparing gas vs electric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for demand variability and reserve capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of great variability in the demand for light at different seasons of the year and at different hours of the day, a comparison must consider the hourly/seasonal demand profile and the reserve capacity needed to meet peaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hourly percentage demand profiles (example table provided) to find maximum simultaneous burners; size plant and reserve so peak demand (e.g., 20% of daily make between 5–6 pm) can be met either by forcing engines or by reserve machines; consider how distribution systems affect required reserve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine maximum number of burners from hourly demand profile
rubrics_metrics.description: From the variation in the demand for light by hour (percentages of total daily make), determine the time of greatest consumption and hence the maximum number of burners to be maintained at any one time (example: maximum = 40,000 burners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the daily percentage distribution of demand to compute peak instantaneous load and thereby derive required generating horsepower and mains size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare distribution-system architectures and their operational implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider Edison's multiple-arc distribution (lamps placed on cross-wires between conductors) versus systems including storage-batteries; each has advantages and drawbacks in reserve sizing and handling rapid demand changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how a system's coupling (for quantity vs intensity), mains topology, and the presence or absence of storage batteries affect reserve plant requirements, ability to cope with rapid demand swings, expansion flexibility, and operational handling of engines/boilers.

rubrics_metrics.name: When lacking data, acknowledge limitations (e.g., storage-battery costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A storage-battery-inclusive system may be preferable, but it cannot enter into the present calculation because there are no data with reference to the first cost and depreciation available, and because present secondary batteries do not seem to have yet reached a satisfactory commercial form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about omissions caused by absent or immature technology data; do not include speculative cost figures without reliable sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate gas-works capital on established per-unit ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of such a plant for coal-gas will vary in this country from $2,500 to $4,000 for each million feet of the yearly make, but $3,000 may be taken as a fair average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historically grounded per-unit capital-cost ranges for gas production when scaling; include mains cost (example: $250,000 for mains in a 3-square-mile district) and adjust for expected actual yearly production (e.g., seasonal variability reducing yearly make).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate electric-plant capital by component-level accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate electric plant cost by summing costs of required engines/dynamos, boilers, distributing stations, and mains; e.g., engines priced per indicated horse-power, dynamos costed by material and construction, boilers by $ per horse-power, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break down the electric plant into components (number of stations, dynamos of given horse-power, boilers at $20/horse-power, mains, reserve plant) and cost each component using material costs and construction allowances; the author gives concrete example figures to follow the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use realistic assumptions for lamp-to-horsepower ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: If we take eight sixteen-candle lamps maintained throughout the whole system for each actual horse-power applied to the dynamo-machine, engines with a normal capacity of five thousand horse-power will be required to sustain the maximum number of burners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt explicit lamp-per-horsepower conversion assumptions (with justification) to translate lighting demand into required machine horsepower; state the conversion used so others can replicate or adjust calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define territorial/coastline conventions when calculating area
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal difficulty in making an accurate computation of the area of a large country like the United States arises from the indeterminateness of the expression 'our territorial outline.' Tradition, not law, sets sea-line at three miles; conventions vary (example: a French-English convention crossing mouths of bays/channels not more than ten miles in width).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly adopt a convention for where the coastline is drawn (three-mile limit, cross mouths of bays under a width threshold, include or exclude landlocked waters like Lake Michigan) because different conventions materially change computed area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for elevation and slope effects in geographic area measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: All tracts the measurement of which is taken in degrees and minutes gain in extent as their height above the sea is increased because they lie on a larger sphere; also mountainous districts gain superficial area by reason of the slope of their hills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include corrections for mean elevation and average slopes when converting angular measurements to surface area; quantify gains (examples: Colorado mean elevation 7,050 ft → gain ~44,800 acres; slope estimates give additional area increases) or at least state that omission will bias results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design long-term water-taste/odor monitoring with trained observers
rubrics_metrics.description: Competent persons trained to scientific observation should undertake systematic daily examinations of the water in reservoirs for long periods of time — say for five years — to watch the changes that take place in its condition and the causes of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement multi-year, regular sampling/observational programs with trained personnel to detect temporal trends, identify sources (vegetable decay, plant parts, dead fish, animalcules), and measure relevant chemical indicators (e.g., albuminoid ammonia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat early navigational latitudes with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Early latitudes are generally trustworthy to within a single degree; minutes or fractions of degrees set down by writers anterior to the middle of the eighteenth century are never to be relied upon, and annotations that identify places within one degree by latitude alone cannot properly be cited as authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using historical latitude data, assume accuracy to ~1 degree; do not rely on early minutes/seconds; document instrument and tabular limitations (e.g., instruments graduated in degrees only, obsolete ephemerides updated infrequently) before making precise identifications.
